name: Guava leaf (Psidium guajava)
short: Case title: allergic contact dermatitis from guava tea. Open trial of leaf decoction by mouth (109 adults, acute diarrhoea): no adverse events reported. 2024 review: few trials; safety needs defining.
text: In an open-label randomised trial of guava leaf decoction taken by mouth three times a day for acute infectious diarrhoea in 109 adults aged 18 to 60, no adverse events were reported, and haemoglobin, liver and kidney tests were normal; the comparison group received oral rehydration solution. A randomised, double-blind study of capsules of a guava leaf product standardised for quercetin in 50 adults with acute diarrhoea was designed to assess safety as well as efficacy, but its abstract reports no safety results. A 2024 systematic review found that only three of 23 included articles were clinical trials and says further studies are needed to define the safety of treatment with guava extracts. The cited sources give no safety data for pregnancy, and the abstract of a randomised trial of a Psidium guajava preparation in 62 patients with infantile rotavirus enteritis does not report adverse events. A case report is titled 'Allergic contact dermatitis due to guava tea'; the record has no abstract, so the patient, the part of the plant used for the tea and how the skin was exposed cannot be reported. Interactions (laboratory and animal data only, for guava leaf tea and extract): polyphenols from guava leaf, but not the whole leaf extract, showed some inhibition of drug-metabolising (CYP) enzymes in the laboratory; the tea inhibited these enzymes, and the breakdown of midazolam, less than grapefruit juice did; and in rats the tea did not change warfarin's effect on blood clotting. The authors conclude from these data that the tea is unlikely to interact with drugs, and note that people taking diabetes medicines or warfarin also drink it. No human interaction study was found in the cited sources.
